solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique, linked answer split by the grid); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Hypocritical and acquisitive affection

parts.note: the whole clue describes love shown only for what one can get, like a pet fond of whoever keeps the food store

explanation.surface: A description of fondness that is really greed in disguise.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no wordplay: the phrase is an idiom for affection shown in hope of reward, from the image of a child or pet loving whoever opens the food store.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names insincere fondness displayed only to gain food or favours, which is both hypocritical and acquisitive.

clue.text: Social climber has to jump on horseback first!

indicators.note: says the horseback piece comes ahead of the jumping piece in the answer

parts.note: a rider who is mounted is said to be up
to start is to jump with surprise

explanation.surface: A pushy newcomer apparently has to leap into the saddle before anything else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first' tells you to put the horseback word before the jump word, though the clue gives them the other way round.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who has risen suddenly in rank and acts above their station is a social climber.

clue.text: Show promise with Blake's first poem On Spring

indicators.note: Blake's first is the opening letter of the name Blake

parts.note: an ode is a lyric poem
a well is a spring of water

explanation.surface: William Blake's early verse, a poem titled On Spring, hints at a talent to come.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On Spring' reads like a poem's title, but 'Spring' is a water source and 'On' just links it. The capital S is there to mislead.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that bodes well is a good omen, so the phrase means to look promising.

clue.text: Too partial in a trial sometimes

indicators.note: only part of the words in a trial sometimes is used, a run of letters inside them

explanation.surface: A remark that bias, too, can creep into a court case now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: 'partial' looks like it means biased, a fitting word for a trial, but it says take part of the following words: triAL SOmetimes.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are adverbs meaning in addition or as well.

clue.text: Stupid suggestion heard for how lullaby's to be played

indicators.note: the two words spoken together, dim and innuendo, give the musical term

parts.note: dim means stupid; an innuendo is an insinuating suggestion

explanation.surface: A daft hint is passed on as advice on performing a cradle song.
explanation.walkthrough: Said quickly, 'dim innuendo' sounds just like the Italian musical direction.
explanation.definitionFit: Diminuendo is the score marking for growing gradually softer, apt for a song meant to send a baby to sleep.

clue.text: Ulster town's old periodical (Hibernian originally)

parts.note: a mag is a magazine, a periodical

indicators.note: the first letter of Hibernian is taken

explanation.surface: An Irish town's long-defunct magazine, the Hibernian, is recalled.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after the definition stands for 'is'. Hibernian means Irish, which makes it look like the name of the periodical.
explanation.definitionFit: Omagh is the county town of Tyrone, in the Ulster province of Northern Ireland.

clue.text: Back the last runner? It fails to start!

parts.note: the end is the last part

indicators.note: the runner word loses its opening letter

parts.note: a horse is a runner in a race

explanation.surface: A punter is urged to bet on the rank outsider, which then never leaves the stalls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fails to start' is racing talk for a non-runner, but here it removes the first letter: HORSE becomes ORSE.
explanation.definitionFit: To endorse a candidate or plan is to back it, giving support.

clue.text: Winter starter? On the contrary!

parts.note: swap the season for its opposite and the first course for the last, a cold-season opener becoming a warm-season dessert

explanation.surface: A menu query about a first course for the cold months, then a contradiction.
explanation.walkthrough: Reverse both words: the opposite of winter is summer, and the opposite of a starter is a pudding, the British word for dessert. Summer pudding is a British dessert of berries in a bread case.
explanation.definitionFit: This berry-filled bread dessert is eaten in the warm season at the end of a meal, the exact opposite of a cold-season first course.

clue.text: Describes international chess matches we presume

definitions.text: Describes international chess matches we presume

parts.words: Describes international chess matches we presume
parts.note: top-level international chess is played by players holding the highest title, so their games would be described with the adjective formed from that title

explanation.surface: A guess at the right adjective for chess at the international level.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that the word normally means masterful in general, but literally describes what the top-titled players produce.
explanation.definitionFit: Grandmaster is the top chess title, so play at international level is presumably worthy of such players.

clue.text: Positive aspects of Union power, right and left

parts.note: P is the physics symbol for power
right and left are the two sides

explanation.surface: A trade union's political clout seems to bring good things to both wings of politics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'right and left' are political wings in the surface but simply two sides in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Upsides are the benefits or good points of a situation, the opposite of downsides.

clue.text: Jerome and Eric get trapped wind

indicators.note: the letters are caught inside the run of words Jerome and Eric

explanation.surface: Two men named Jerome and Eric are caught out by a gust or by flatulence.
explanation.walkthrough: The run is jeroME AND ERic. 'wind' is a verb rhyming with 'find', not the breeze.
explanation.definitionFit: To wind is to twist and turn along a course, as a river or path does.

clue.text: It could be a queen's demand

definitions.text: It could be a queen's demand

parts.words: It could be a queen's demand
parts.note: a queen is also a female cat, whose demand for food is her call

explanation.surface: A royal command, it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: A queen is a female cat, so her demand is her cry.
explanation.definitionFit: The cry of a cat asking to be fed or let out, and a queen is a female cat.

clue.text: Like fugitives, one after the other

definitions.meaning: escapees are being hunted and keep moving
in quick succession, one thing following another without a break

explanation.surface: Escapees running in single file.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both fleeing from pursuit and done hurriedly in succession.

clue.text: Labour's aim seen as light- hearted competition

definitions.meaning: the purpose of labour in childbirth is a baby's arrival
a cheerful contest or occasion, read literally as a joyful event

explanation.surface: The Labour Party's goal is presented as a jolly contest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour' with a capital looks like the British political party, but it is labour in childbirth.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a euphemism for a birth, and read literally it is a joyful sporting fixture.

clue.text: Fights back at earliest upset

indicators.note: the letters of at earliest are knocked over into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone retaliates as soon as they are upset.
explanation.definitionFit: To retaliate is to strike back against an attacker, the same as fighting back.

clue.text: Bug starts to get everyone really morbid

indicators.note: the opening letter of each of the next four words is taken

explanation.surface: An illness bug is starting to make everyone feel very gloomy.
explanation.definitionFit: A bug in the sense of an infection is a microbe causing disease.

clue.text: Split in head of door nail that makes holes bigger

indicators.note: the split word goes inside the letters made from the head of door and the nail
the first letter of door is taken

parts.note: a pin is a slender nail
a rift is a split or crack

explanation.surface: A crack running through the top of a door near a nail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts RIFT inside DPIN (D from the head of door, plus PIN). 'that makes holes bigger' defines a tool.
explanation.definitionFit: A tapered steel pin driven into a hole to enlarge or align it with another, as in metalwork or riveting.

clue.text: Ill-treated sailor, deserting, given employment

indicators.note: the sailor leaves the ill-treated word

parts.note: abused means ill-treated
AB, able seaman, is a sailor

explanation.surface: A mistreated sailor goes AWOL and finds a job elsewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deserting' fits a sailor jumping ship, which is just what happens to AB here.
explanation.definitionFit: Something given employment has been put to use, so it has been employed.

clue.text: Thrills with old spectacles reportedly

parts.note: ex means former or old

indicators.note: the word for spectacles is spoken, giving a word with the same sound

parts.note: sights are spectacles, things to see

explanation.surface: Someone is thrilled, it's said, by antique eyeglasses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spectacles' looks like glasses but means sights, which sound like CITES.
explanation.definitionFit: To excite someone is to stir them up with eagerness, so it thrills them.

clue.text: Flycatchers — the stationary kind

parts.note: a flycatcher is a bird that hunts on the wing, while a static trap of silk spun by an arachnid catches flies without moving

explanation.surface: A bird-watcher's note on flycatchers that stay put.
explanation.walkthrough: Flycatchers are songbirds, but the clue wants something that catches flies while staying fixed in place.
explanation.definitionFit: Webs spun by arachnids trap flying insects without moving, so they are fixed fly-catchers.

clue.text: Boards require English grades to contain a B

indicators.note: the grades word holds the letter B within it

parts.note: marks are grades given for work
taken as written

explanation.surface: School boards set the rule that English grades must include a B.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boards' looks like an exam board noun, but it is the verb, as in getting onto a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: To embark is to go aboard a ship or plane, so it boards.

clue.text: Deceased associate wasted millions this month

indicators.note: the associate word loses its millions letter

parts.note: a member is an associate of a club

explanation.surface: A late partner squandered a fortune in the current month.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wasted' suggests squandering money, but it removes M from MEMBER, leaving EMBER. The clue was published in that month.
explanation.definitionFit: The puzzle appeared in the twelfth month, so the date of publication is the definition.

clue.text: For me, Blair can show guts

indicators.note: the letters of for me Blair can be rearranged to show something new

explanation.surface: A supporter credits Tony Blair with having the nerve to act.
explanation.walkthrough: Tony Blair was the British Labour prime minister from 1997 to 2007.
explanation.definitionFit: Guts means courage, and moral fibre is strength of character to do what is right.

clue.text: See 23
Where to hide from landlord when penniless

indicators.note: the landlord loses D, the old abbreviation for a penny

parts.note: a laird is a Scottish landlord

explanation.surface: A tenant who is broke hides from the landlord.
explanation.walkthrough: A LAIRD is a Scottish landowner. D stood for a penny in pre-decimal British money.
explanation.definitionFit: A lair is an animal's den or a person's hideout, a place to hide.

clue.text: Teachers Peg, including Romeo and Hazel, say

parts.note: NUT was the National Union of Teachers in Britain

indicators.note: the peg word takes the Romeo letter inside it

parts.note: a tee is a golfer's peg
R is Romeo in the radio alphabet

explanation.surface: A school staffroom roll call naming Peg, Romeo and Hazel.
explanation.walkthrough: Peg, Romeo and Hazel all look like names; 'Hazel, say' is the definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: The hazel bears hazelnuts, so it is an example of a tree grown for its nuts.

clue.text: Fancy gear mostly obvious on the left

indicators.note: most of the obvious word is kept, its tail dropped

parts.note: apparent means obvious
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: Showy kit that's plainly on the left-hand side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' just joins the pieces. 'mostly' cuts the last two letters from APPARENT, giving APPARE.
explanation.definitionFit: Apparel is formal clothing, especially fine or ornate dress.

clue.text: Arsonists lie about beiing lonely

indicators.note: the letters of arsonists lie are moved about into a new order

explanation.surface: Fire-raisers lie to cover up their isolation.
explanation.definitionFit: Solitariness is the state of being alone, which is the condition of being lonely.
